name: Chapter 5: Thermodynamics
description: Systems, first law, work and heat, enthalpy, calorimetry, Hess’s law, bond and lattice enthalpy, entropy, Gibbs energy and equilibrium

cards.definition: System: the part being studied. Surroundings: the rest that can interact. Universe = system + surroundings.
The real or imaginary wall separating system from surroundings; tracks matter and energy flow
Open (open beaker): Matter and energy; Closed (sealed copper vessel): Energy only; Isolated (thermos flask): Neither

cards.term: Is heat (q) or work (w) a state function?
cards.definition: No: both are path functions; but q + w = ΔU is

cards.term: Everyday example of a state function? (NCERT)
cards.definition: Volume of water in a pond: same whether filled by rain or tubewell
Total energy of the system (chemical, electrical, mechanical…); only ΔU can be measured
Heat flows in/out, work is done on/by the system, matter enters/leaves
No heat transfer between system and surroundings (adiabatic wall)

cards.term: What did Joule’s paddle/immersion-rod experiments show?
cards.definition: The same adiabatic work, done any way, gives the same change of state: ΔU = w_ad, so U is a state function

cards.text: IUPAC sign convention: w is {{c1::positive}} when work is done on the system; q is {{c2::positive}} when heat flows into the system.
cards.extra: Trap: many physics books use the old convention (work done BY the system positive).

cards.term: When heat flows through conducting walls with no work, ΔU = ?
cards.definition: q
\( \Delta U = q + w \): energy of an isolated system is constant

cards.term: Problem 5.1: ΔU for (i) adiabatic, work done on; (ii) heat lost, no work; (iii) work by system, heat supplied?
cards.definition: (i) ΔU = w_ad (adiabatic wall). (ii) ΔU = −q (conducting wall). (iii) ΔU = q − w (closed system).
\( w = -p_{ex} \Delta V = -p_{ex}(V_f - V_i) \)

cards.term: On a p-V plot, what does work on the gas equal?
cards.definition: The shaded area under the curve
One that can be reversed at any moment by an infinitesimal change; proceeds infinitely slowly through equilibrium states

cards.term: Reversible isothermal work for an ideal gas?
cards.definition: \( w_{rev} = -2.303 \, nRT \log \frac{V_f}{V_i} \)

cards.term: What is free expansion, and the work done?
cards.definition: Expansion into vacuum (p_ex = 0): w = 0, reversible or not

cards.term: For isothermal expansion of an ideal gas, ΔU = ?
cards.definition: 0 (U depends only on T), so q = −w

cards.term: Why does reversible expansion give the most work? (intuition)
cards.definition: The gas always pushes against the largest possible opposing pressure; area under the curve is maximum

cards.term: 2 L gas at 10 atm expands isothermally into vacuum to 10 L. q and w? (Problem 5.2)
cards.definition: q = w = 0
q = −w = 1 × 8 = 8 L atm
39.37 L atm

advancedHtml.frontHtml:
Problem 5.4

1 mol gas, 2 L → 10 L reversibly at 298 K. q?

q = −w = 2.303 nRT log(V_f/V_i)
  1. V_f/V_i = 10/2 = 5
  2. q = 2.303 × 1 × 0.08206 × 298 × log 5
  3. = 2.303 × 0.08206 × 298 × 0.699
  4. ?
advancedHtml.backHtml:
Problem 5.4

1 mol gas, 2 L → 10 L reversibly at 298 K. q?

q = −w = 2.303 nRT log(V_f/V_i)
  1. V_f/V_i = 10/2 = 5
  2. q = 2.303 × 1 × 0.08206 × 298 × log 5
  3. = 2.303 × 0.08206 × 298 × 0.699
  4. = 39.37 L atm

cards.term: Relation between ΔH and ΔU for gaseous reactions?
cards.definition: \( \Delta H = \Delta U + \Delta n_g RT \)
Moles of gaseous products − gaseous reactants
For solids/liquids only, or when Δn_g = 0 (e.g. H₂ + Cl₂ → 2HCl)

cards.term: ΔU for vaporising 1 mol water at 100 °C if ΔvapH = 41 kJ/mol? (Problem 5.5)

cards.definition: Δn_g = −2, so ΔH < ΔU
Extensive: depends on amount (mass, V, U, H, C). Intensive: does not (T, p, density).

cards.term: Is a molar property extensive or intensive?
cards.definition: Intensive (e.g. molar volume, molar heat capacity)

cards.term: Heat capacity, molar heat capacity and specific heat?
cards.definition: C: q = CΔT. Cₘ: per mole. Specific heat c: per unit mass, q = c·m·ΔT.

cards.term: Relation between Cp and Cv for an ideal gas?

cards.definition: At constant p, part of the heat does expansion work, so more heat is needed per degree

cards.term: Which calorimeter measures ΔU, and why?
cards.definition: The bomb calorimeter: sealed steel bomb, constant volume, so q_V = ΔU
A constant-pressure calorimeter (e.g. coffee-cup / foamed polystyrene cup)
−248 kJ/mol

advancedHtml.frontHtml:
Problem 5.6

1 g graphite burnt in bomb calorimeter, C = 20.7 kJ/K, T 298 → 299 K. ΔH?

q = −C·ΔT; scale to 1 mol; Δn_g = 0.
  1. q(1 g) = −20.7 × 1 = −20.7 kJ
  2. ?
  3. Δn_g = 0, so ΔH = ΔU = −2.48 × 10² kJ mol⁻¹
advancedHtml.backHtml:
Problem 5.6

1 g graphite burnt in bomb calorimeter, C = 20.7 kJ/K, T 298 → 299 K. ΔH?

q = −C·ΔT; scale to 1 mol; Δn_g = 0.
  1. q(1 g) = −20.7 × 1 = −20.7 kJ
  2. Per mol: −20.7 × 12 = −248 kJ
  3. Δn_g = 0, so ΔH = ΔU = −2.48 × 10² kJ mol⁻¹

cards.term: Sign of ΔrH for exothermic and endothermic reactions?
cards.definition: Exothermic: negative; endothermic: positive
\( \Delta_r H = \sum a_i H_{products} - \sum b_i H_{reactants} \)
Pure form at 1 bar and the specified temperature (usually 298 K)

cards.text: Phase-change enthalpies: melting = {{c1::ΔfusH}}, boiling = {{c2::ΔvapH}}, solid → vapour = {{c3::ΔsubH}}; all are {{c4::positive}}.

cards.term: Why does acetone need less heat to vaporise than water?
cards.definition: Water has strong H-bonds; acetone only weaker dipole-dipole forces

cards.term: Heat to evaporate 18 g water at 298 K, and ΔvapU? (Problem 5.7)
cards.definition: q = 44.01 kJ; ΔU = 44.01 − 2.48 = 41.53 kJ

Problem 5.8

1 mol water at 100 °C → ice at 0 °C. ΔU? (ΔfusH = 6.00 kJ/mol, c = 4.2 J/g°C)

Cool the liquid, then freeze.
  1. ΔH₁ = −18 × 4.2 × 100 = −7.56 kJ
  2. ΔH₂ = −6.00 kJ
  3. ?
advancedHtml.backHtml:
Problem 5.8

1 mol water at 100 °C → ice at 0 °C. ΔU? (ΔfusH = 6.00 kJ/mol, c = 4.2 J/g°C)

Cool the liquid, then freeze.
  1. ΔH₁ = −18 × 4.2 × 100 = −7.56 kJ
  2. ΔH₂ = −6.00 kJ
  3. ΔH = −13.56 kJ; no gas, so ΔU = −13.56 kJ mol⁻¹

cards.term: Define standard enthalpy of formation ΔfH°.
cards.definition: Enthalpy change to form one mole of a compound from its elements in their most stable states

cards.term: Reference states of H, O, C, S?
cards.definition: H₂(g), O₂(g), C (graphite), S (rhombic)

cards.term: ΔfH° of an element in its reference state?
cards.definition: Zero by convention

cards.term: Why is CaO + CO₂ → CaCO₃ not ΔfH of CaCO₃?
cards.definition: CaCO₃ is formed from compounds, not from elements

cards.term: Why is H₂ + Br₂ → 2HBr not ΔfH of HBr?
cards.definition: It forms 2 mol: ΔfH(HBr) = ½ of it = −36.4 kJ/mol
−285.8, −74.81, −393.5 kJ mol⁻¹

(−635.1) + (−393.5) − (−1206.9) = +178.3 kJ mol⁻¹: endothermic
A balanced equation with physical states and its ΔrH

cards.text: Thermochemical rules: coefficients mean {{c1::moles}} (never molecules); halving the equation {{c2::halves}} ΔrH; reversing it {{c3::reverses the sign}}.

cards.term: Hess’s law of constant heat summation?
cards.definition: ΔrH is the same whether a reaction occurs in one step or many (H is a state function)

cards.term: Hess: enthalpy of formation of CO
cards.definition: −110.5 kJ/mol

advancedHtml.frontHtml:
Hess’s law

ΔrH for C(graphite) + ½O₂ → CO?

C + O₂ → CO₂: −393.5. CO + ½O₂ → CO₂: −283.0.
  1. Reverse the second: CO₂ → CO + ½O₂, +283.0
  2. Add to the first
  3. ?
advancedHtml.backHtml:
Hess’s law

ΔrH for C(graphite) + ½O₂ → CO?

C + O₂ → CO₂: −393.5. CO + ½O₂ → CO₂: −283.0.
  1. Reverse the second: CO₂ → CO + ½O₂, +283.0
  2. Add to the first
  3. ΔrH = −393.5 + 283.0 = −110.5 kJ mol⁻¹

cards.term: Why can’t ΔfH of CO be measured directly?
cards.definition: Burning carbon always gives some CO₂ along with CO

advancedHtml.frontHtml:
Problem 5.9

ΔcH(benzene) = −3267 kJ/mol. ΔfH(benzene)? (ΔfH CO₂ −393.5, H₂O −285.83)

C₆H₆ + 15/2 O₂ → 6CO₂ + 3H₂O
  1. 6(−393.5) + 3(−285.83) = −3218.5
  2. ΔfH = −3218.5 − (−3267.0)
  3. ?
advancedHtml.backHtml:
Problem 5.9

ΔcH(benzene) = −3267 kJ/mol. ΔfH(benzene)? (ΔfH CO₂ −393.5, H₂O −285.83)

C₆H₆ + 15/2 O₂ → 6CO₂ + 3H₂O
  1. 6(−393.5) + 3(−285.83) = −3218.5
  2. ΔfH = −3218.5 − (−3267.0)
  3. = +48.5 kJ mol⁻¹

cards.term: Correction: NCERT’s Problem 5.9 working prints the final ΔfH(benzene) with a minus sign. Right sign?
cards.definition: +48.5 kJ/mol: −3218.5 − (−3267.0) is positive; reversing the combustion equation gives +3267, not −3267
Enthalpy change to break one mole of bonds completely into gaseous atoms (e.g. H₂ → 2H, 435 kJ/mol; CH₄ → C + 4H, 1665 kJ/mol)

cards.term: For Na(s) → Na(g), atomization enthalpy equals?
cards.definition: Enthalpy of sublimation (108.4 kJ/mol)

cards.term: Bond dissociation enthalpy vs mean bond enthalpy?
cards.definition: Dissociation: for a specific bond. Mean: average over identical bonds, e.g. C–H in CH₄ = 1665/4 = 416 kJ/mol.

cards.term: Why do the 4 C–H bonds of CH₄ need different energies (427, 439, 452, 347)?
cards.definition: Each step breaks a bond in a different fragment (CH₄, CH₃, CH₂, CH)

cards.term: Bond enthalpies of H–H, Cl–Cl, O=O?
cards.definition: 435, 242, 498 kJ/mol (Table 5.3; the text says 428 for O=O)
\( \Delta_r H = \sum BE_{reactants} - \sum BE_{products} \) (bonds broken − bonds formed)

cards.term: Trap: order of terms in the bond-enthalpy formula vs the ΔfH formula?
cards.definition: Bond enthalpies: reactants − products. Formation enthalpies: products − reactants.
Enthalpy change when 1 mol of an ionic solid dissociates into gaseous ions (NaCl: +788 kJ/mol)
Indirectly, by a Born-Haber cycle (Hess’s law; sum round a cycle = 0)

cards.text: Born-Haber for NaCl: ΔlatticeH = {{c1::411.2}} (−ΔfH) + {{c2::108.4}} (ΔsubH Na) + {{c3::121}} (½ Cl–Cl) + {{c4::496}} (ΔiH Na) − {{c5::348.6}} (ΔegH Cl) = 788 kJ/mol.

cards.definition: Energies are defined at 0 K; ΔiH = E₀ + 5/2 RT; ΔegH = −A − 5/2 RT

cards.term: Enthalpy of solution from lattice and hydration enthalpy?
cards.definition: \( \Delta_{sol} H = \Delta_{lattice} H + \Delta_{hyd} H \); NaCl: 788 − 784 = +4 kJ/mol

cards.term: Why does solubility of most salts rise with temperature?
cards.definition: ΔsolH is usually positive (endothermic dissolution)

cards.term: Why are many fluorides less soluble than chlorides?
cards.definition: Small F⁻ gives a very high lattice enthalpy
Heat change on adding more solvent to a solution, e.g. HCl·25aq + 15aq → HCl·40aq: −0.76 kJ/mol

cards.term: Enthalpy of solution at infinite dilution for HCl?
cards.definition: −74.85 kJ/mol (limiting value as solvent increases)
Has the potential to proceed without external help; says nothing about rate (H₂ + O₂ at room T)
No: it is irreversible and can be reversed only by an external agency

cards.term: Is decrease in enthalpy enough for spontaneity?
cards.definition: No: some endothermic reactions are spontaneous (e.g. ½N₂ + O₂ → NO₂; C + 2S → CS₂)

cards.term: Enthalpy diagram of an exothermic reaction?
cards.definition: Products lie below reactants; ΔrH negative

cards.term: What drives diffusion of two gases when ΔH = 0?
cards.definition: Increase in entropy (disorder)

cards.term: Entropy change for a reversible process?
cards.definition: \( \Delta S = \frac{q_{rev}}{T} \)

cards.term: Why does heat added at low T raise entropy more? (intuition)
cards.definition: A cold system is ordered, so the same heat causes a bigger relative increase in randomness (like a sneeze in a quiet library vs a busy street)

cards.term: Entropy order of solid, liquid, gas?
cards.definition: Solid < liquid < gas

cards.term: Criterion for spontaneity in terms of entropy?
cards.definition: \( \Delta S_{total} = \Delta S_{sys} + \Delta S_{surr} > 0 \); at equilibrium ΔS_total = 0

cards.term: Does ΔU distinguish reversible from irreversible expansion?
cards.definition: No (ΔU = 0 for both isothermally); ΔS_total does

cards.term: Entropy increases or decreases? (i) liquid → solid, (ii) solid 0 → 115 K, (iii) NaHCO₃ decomposes, (iv) H₂ → 2H. (Problem 5.10)
cards.definition: (i) decreases; (ii), (iii), (iv) increase
ΔS_total = +4980.6 J/K/mol

ΔS_surr = −ΔH/T
  1. ΔS_surr = 1648 × 10³ / 298 = 5530 J/K/mol
  2. ?

advancedHtml.backHtml:
Problem 5.11

4Fe + 3O₂ → 2Fe₂O₃: ΔS = −549.4 J/K/mol, ΔH = −1648 kJ/mol. Why spontaneous?

ΔS_surr = −ΔH/T
  1. ΔS_surr = 1648 × 10³ / 298 = 5530 J/K/mol
  2. ΔS_total = 5530 − 549.4
  3. = +4980.6 J/K/mol > 0, spontaneous

cards.definition: \( G = H - TS \); extensive state function
\( \Delta G = \Delta H - T \Delta S \)

cards.text: At constant T and p: ΔG {{c1::< 0}} → spontaneous; ΔG {{c2::> 0}} → non-spontaneous; ΔG {{c3::= 0}} → equilibrium.

cards.definition: ΔG is the net energy available for useful work (TΔS is unavailable)
ΔH−ΔS+: always; ΔH+ΔS+: high T; ΔH−ΔS−: low T; ΔH+ΔS−: never

cards.definition: \( T = \frac{\Delta H}{\Delta S} \)

cards.term: Why are spontaneous exothermic reactions so common?
cards.definition: Released heat increases the entropy of the surroundings
Entropy of a pure perfect crystal → 0 as T → 0 K

cards.term: Why is the third law limited to pure crystals?
cards.definition: Solutions and supercooled liquids have non-zero entropy at 0 K
Lets us find absolute entropies from thermal data

cards.definition: Much greater than 1: reaction goes nearly to completion

advancedHtml.frontHtml:
Problem 5.14

N₂O₄ ⇌ 2NO₂ is 50% dissociated at 60 °C, 1 atm. ΔG°?

Start with 1 mol N₂O₄.
  1. Mol: N₂O₄ 0.5, NO₂ 1.0; total 1.5
  2. Kp = (1/1.5)² / (0.5/1.5) = 1.33 atm
  3. ΔG° = −2.303 × 8.314 × 333 × log 1.33
  4. ?
advancedHtml.backHtml:
Problem 5.14

N₂O₄ ⇌ 2NO₂ is 50% dissociated at 60 °C, 1 atm. ΔG°?

Start with 1 mol N₂O₄.
  1. Mol: N₂O₄ 0.5, NO₂ 1.0; total 1.5
  2. Kp = (1/1.5)² / (0.5/1.5) = 1.33 atm
  3. ΔG° = −2.303 × 8.314 × 333 × log 1.33
  4. = ≈ −790 J mol⁻¹ (−0.79 kJ mol⁻¹)

cards.term: Correction: NCERT prints ΔG° = −763.8 kJ/mol in Problem 5.14. Right answer?
cards.definition: 2.303 × 8.314 × 333 × 0.1239 ≈ 790 J, so ΔG° ≈ −0.79 kJ/mol. Sanity check: K ≈ 1 always means ΔG° ≈ 0, never hundreds of kJ.
